frictionVectors.title: EUROPEAN GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over its hydrocarbon sector and pipeline infrastructure, giving it leverage with European buyers. Price volatility, European diversification, and investment demands constrain that leverage.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Instability across the Sahel and competing Russian, Western, and regional security initiatives challenge Algeria's non-interventionist posture and border security.

frictionVectors.title: OIL CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Angola controls its petroleum institutions but remains heavily dependent on foreign operators, offshore technology, and volatile crude revenues. Declining production and debt-service pressures narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE FINANCE LEGACY
frictionVectors.details: Major transport and energy infrastructure remains linked to Chinese contractors and earlier oil-backed financing. Luanda is diversifying partnerships, but refinancing and maintenance obligations preserve external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: NIGER BORDER DISRUPTION
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger and militant activity in the tri-border zone threaten northern trade routes, energy projects, and state access. Security cooperation and border infrastructure remain vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Benin's economy and regional influence depend heavily on the Port of Cotonou and transit trade with neighbors. External logistics, financing, and security partnerships create exposure despite expanding state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: DIAMOND MARKET CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured stronger negotiating leverage with major diamond partners, but public revenues remain exposed to global demand and synthetic-diamond competition. Diversification beyond diamonds is strategically urgent.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS CAPACITY
frictionVectors.details: New copper, nickel, and other mineral opportunities could strengthen sovereign control if processing and transport capacity improve. Foreign capital and limited domestic infrastructure remain the main constraints.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The junta's pursuit of Russian security support reduces reliance on Western partners but introduces new external dependencies and limited transparency. The arrangement has not eliminated militant threats to mining zones and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTROL CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and local value capture from gold, while insecurity disrupts production and logistics. Foreign operators face regulatory uncertainty, taxation pressure, and elevated physical risk.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–Burundi Security Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border destabilization continue to constrain trade and security cooperation. Tensions also complicate Burundi’s management of eastern DRC-linked mineral and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control and revenue from nickel, rare earths, and other mining projects, but limited capital and technical capacity leave it reliant on foreign investors and opaque intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde’s maritime security and port relevance attract sustained U.S., European, and Chinese interest. The government must balance partnerships without allowing strategic infrastructure or basing access to become politically divisive.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Maritime Enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing threatens sovereign control over marine resources. Limited patrol capacity leaves the archipelago dependent on European and international surveillance support.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons, timber, and mining remain central to state finances, while weak transparency and elite-controlled licensing limit broad domestic benefits. External firms retain significant influence over extraction, logistics, and technical services.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Corridor Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest regions continues to disrupt agricultural, transport, and energy investment. Instability around the Far North and major regional corridors also raises dependence on foreign security and infrastructure partners.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-for-Resources Model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel remain central to regime protection and counterinsurgency, reinforcing Moscow’s political access. Mining concessions and commercial privileges are widely viewed as part of the broader security bargain.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Weak state control outside Bangui enables armed groups, foreign traders, and informal networks to capture value from gold and diamonds. Poor transport infrastructure further limits formal taxation and national oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Dependence and Contract Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Crude exports underpin public finance and political stability, but production and infrastructure remain dependent on foreign operators and external transit arrangements. Revenue volatility constrains sovereign investment in diversification and basic services.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and External Patronage
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict has intensified refugee flows, arms trafficking, and pressure on Chad’s eastern provinces. N’Djamena is balancing ties with Gulf states, France, Russia-linked actors, and regional partners while seeking to avoid direct entanglement.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' effective control over nearby maritime space and migration policy.

frictionVectors.title: External economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Remittances, donor funding, and imported fuel underpin the economy, leaving infrastructure and energy security vulnerable to outside leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern armed conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving the M23 rebellion and regional actors continues to weaken Kinshasa's control over territory, transport corridors, and mineral zones in the east.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and American interests compete for copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals while governance and local value capture remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State revenue and export earnings remain heavily dependent on offshore oil, exposing sovereignty and public finances to price cycles and foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, energy, and industrial projects expand connectivity but increase dependence on external finance, contractors, and commodity-linked repayment structures.

highlights: Cocoa and gold remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Commodity value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening processing and infrastructure, but cocoa and gold revenues remain vulnerable to foreign pricing, certification rules, and multinational buyers.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist spillover from the Sahel threatens northern transport corridors and requires expanding security cooperation with regional and external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's logistics economy relies on foreign-backed port infrastructure and Ethiopian trade, creating exposure to creditor, operator, and regional demand pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Military competition in the Red Sea
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of Chinese, American, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generates revenue but narrows policy flexibility amid Red Sea and Gulf rivalries.

highlights: Suez corridor remains a strategic revenue pillar
Gulf and IMF capital deepen fiscal dependence

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-AND-ASSET PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs give Gulf investors and international lenders leverage over state assets and economic policy. Privatization and foreign-exchange reforms can improve liquidity while narrowing sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: NILE WATER SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt exposed to upstream operating decisions and wider Red Sea and Horn instability.

frictionVectors.title: MATURE OIL AND GAS ASSETS
frictionVectors.details: Declining reserves and dependence on foreign technical operators constrain Malabo's bargaining power. LNG infrastructure provides leverage but also locks the economy into external capital and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Maritime security, shipping access, and offshore investment remain vulnerable to regional piracy risks and competition among external energy partners.

highlights: State retains unusually tight control over strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: MINING PARTNERSHIP DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production relies on foreign companies, equipment, and markets, limiting domestic value capture despite strong political control over licensing.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA STRATEGIC PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the conflict in Sudan and Yemen attract competing external security interests. Port and maritime development remain constrained by sanctions exposure and regional instability.

highlights: Economic sovereignty remains tied to South African systems
Sugar, timber, and manufacturing retain limited leverage

frictionVectors.title: SOUTH AFRICAN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Imports, banking channels, electricity, logistics, and labor-market access are heavily linked to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. This supports stability but sharply limits independent economic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: TEXTILE PREFERENCE RISK
frictionVectors.details: Export manufacturing remains exposed to shifts in United States trade preferences and global apparel sourcing, leaving jobs and foreign exchange vulnerable to external policy decisions.

highlights: GERD strengthens control over future power exports
Debt and conflict constrain strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: NILE NEGOTIATION DEADLOCK
frictionVectors.details: The GERD gives Ethiopia greater control over electricity generation and regional leverage, but unresolved operating rules continue to drive confrontation with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Railways, telecoms, power, and industrial projects depend on foreign lenders, contractors, and restructuring arrangements. Debt pressure limits Addis Ababa's ability to convert strategic infrastructure into fully sovereign assets.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Resource Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-coup authorities are seeking greater state influence over oil, manganese, and other strategic assets while preserving foreign investment. Unclear contract terms and institutional weakness could limit the practical gains in sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon remains reliant on foreign capital, technical expertise, and regional diplomatic support during its political transition. France, China, and Gulf-linked investors retain significant commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Economic Penetration
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, energy, and security links with Senegal are essential to Gambian stability but constrain policy autonomy. Border and fisheries disputes periodically expose the asymmetry in the relationship.

frictionVectors.title: Fragile Revenue Base
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia remains dependent on tourism, remittances, and external assistance, leaving strategic infrastructure and public finance vulnerable to outside donors. Limited domestic capacity restricts control over fisheries and port-related resources.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Governance and Illegal Gold
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining continues to damage land and water systems while diverting gold revenues from the formal state economy. Efforts to increase domestic processing and tighten licensing face entrenched local and commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Investor Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stabilization and debt restructuring improve macroeconomic room but reduce policy flexibility in the near term. External lenders and investors retain influence over energy, mining, and infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite, iron ore, and related rail and port projects are driving growth, but Chinese, Emirati, and other foreign firms retain major roles in financing, logistics, and processing. The state captures revenue while remaining dependent on external infrastructure and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Junta Legitimacy and Contract Risk
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities use resource nationalism to build legitimacy but have not fully resolved the transition to civilian rule. Political uncertainty raises the risk of opaque concessions, delayed projects, and social conflict around mining zones.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Dependency
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, exposing farmers and state revenues to foreign traders, price swings, and weak processing capacity. Limited infrastructure prevents Guinea-Bissau from capturing substantial value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Narcotics and Political Capture
frictionVectors.details: Transnational cocaine trafficking continues to exploit weak institutions, porous maritime routes, and political protection networks. This undermines sovereign control over ports, customs, and security institutions.

highlights: Geothermal expansion strengthens domestic energy security

frictionVectors.title: Sovereign Debt and External Financing
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed fiscal reforms and large external repayments constrain Nairobi's policy space. Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders compete for influence over infrastructure and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Mombasa–Northern Corridor remains vital but faces competition from Tanzanian routes and external investment interests. Control over logistics pricing and connectivity remains politically sensitive.

highlights: Water exports remain the core strategic asset
Economic dependence on South Africa persists

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water revenues and infrastructure are closely tied to South African demand and financing. Delays, cost overruns, or disputes could weaken Maseru's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Bordered Economic Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Trade, remittances, electricity, and employment are heavily linked to South Africa, limiting independent economic maneuver. Textile exports also remain vulnerable to external market access.

highlights: Mining revival attracts competing foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and gold development depend on foreign operators and concession finance, creating persistent risks around revenue capture, local content, and contract transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Transport Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Modernization of ports, roads, and power systems relies heavily on external investors and donors. Infrastructure deals could improve capacity while narrowing future policy flexibility.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided by rival authorities
Foreign security and energy actors shape access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and revenue distribution. International oil companies and external sponsors retain substantial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: External security partnerships and mercenary-linked networks complicate national control of borders, bases, and energy corridors. Rival outside actors can amplify local disruptions.

highlights: Critical minerals draw intense foreign interest
Energy and transport gaps limit value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining Revenue and Contract Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented infrastructure. Fiscal returns and environmental safeguards remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages, weak transport links, and port constraints increase reliance on external financiers and project operators. This reduces Madagascar's ability to process resources domestically.

highlights: Debt restructuring opens a narrow reform window

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Debt distress and persistent foreign-exchange shortages leave Lilongwe reliant on IMF, donor, and creditor support, limiting policy autonomy over strategic infrastructure and imports.

frictionVectors.title: MINING GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium, rare-earth, and niobium projects could diversify exports, but weak regulatory capacity raises concerns over concession terms, local value capture, and foreign operator dominance.

highlights: State seeks a larger share of gold revenues
Russian security ties deepen strategic dependence

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SOVEREIGNTY DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is renegotiating mining terms and pressing foreign operators for greater state participation, creating recurring disputes with international companies over taxes, licenses, and operational control.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY FOOTPRINT
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support provides the junta with political cover but increases exposure to opaque contracting, sanctions risk, and external influence over strategic assets.

highlights: Offshore gas is reshaping national leverage
Iron and green-hydrogen plans attract competing investors

frictionVectors.title: GAS REVENUE AND CROSS-BORDER COORDINATION
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers new fiscal leverage, but production delays, revenue-sharing arrangements, and cross-border governance remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN-CAPITAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, port, renewable-energy, and prospective green-hydrogen projects depend heavily on multinational finance and technology, limiting Mauritania's bargaining power despite its resource base.

highlights: Stable institutions protect maritime bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND MARITIME SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos settlement and future administration of the archipelago remain central to Mauritius's sovereignty agenda, while external military and strategic interests constrain its room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CABLE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius seeks to expand as an Indian Ocean logistics and data hub, but competition among India, China, Gulf investors, and Western partners creates pressure over port access and critical connectivity.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables strengthen strategic autonomy
Western Sahara remains the core sovereignty front

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Rabat's control of the territory and its fisheries, phosphate, port, and renewable assets continues to generate legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some European stakeholders.

frictionVectors.title: WATER AND ENERGY SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Drought, desalination needs, and reliance on imported energy complicate Morocco's sovereignty gains from phosphates, solar power, and green-hydrogen investment.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Insurgency Still Constrains Sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The LNG revival depends heavily on international operators, lenders, and security support, limiting Maputo's leverage over project timing and revenue terms.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Gap
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks and localized instability continue to threaten gas infrastructure, displace communities, and expand reliance on foreign military assistance.

highlights: Critical Minerals and Green Hydrogen Push

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Emerging Energy Assets
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate capital and technical capacity in offshore oil and green-hydrogen projects, creating future bargaining risks over local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Export-Corridor Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, and electricity limitations could leave Namibia dependent on external infrastructure partners and neighboring transit routes.

highlights: Uranium and Oil Operations Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Export Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with foreign mining interests and border insecurity threaten uranium, oil, and gold production while reducing reliable access to export corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependency
frictionVectors.details: The junta's turn toward Russian security support increases strategic autonomy from Western partners but risks opaque resource concessions and weakened institutional oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Militancy
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, illegal refining, and renewed instability in the Niger Delta continue to erode state control and reduce fiscal returns from hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria remains reliant on foreign finance, technology, and operators for deepwater production, gas infrastructure, and grid expansion despite stronger domestic refining capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Backlash
frictionVectors.details: Accusations that Rwanda facilitates mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo expose Kigali to sanctions, diplomatic pressure, and supply-chain restrictions.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's development model remains linked to foreign aid and investment, while overseas criticism of its regional military posture threatens economic and diplomatic space.

highlights: Maritime hydrocarbons remain prospective, not yet transformative
External partners shape Gulf of Guinea security

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resource Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Oil prospects and maritime-boundary questions attract foreign energy interest, but limited state capacity constrains São Tomé and Príncipe's ability to set terms independently.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Maritime Enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and dependence on external patrol, surveillance, and development support weaken effective control over the country's maritime zone.

highlights: Resource nationalism meets fiscal and contractual pressure

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers Dakar greater leverage over international operators, while debt, financing obligations, and technical dependence limit how quickly local control can expand.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy corridors, and logistics projects draw Gulf, European, Chinese, and other external capital, creating strategic choices over ownership and long-term revenue capture.

highlights: Blue economy remains the sovereignty anchor

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Fisheries Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains regulatory authority over its waters, but foreign fleets, processing capacity, and market access can capture much of the value generated by marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Maritime surveillance and port access involve cooperation with India, France, and other partners, requiring careful balancing to avoid strategic overdependence.

highlights: Local processing remains the sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Dominated Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, diamonds, and other minerals generate state revenue, but foreign capital, equipment, marketing networks, and concession structures limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Export infrastructure tied to mining projects can improve connectivity while also giving external investors influence over strategic transport corridors and bargaining power with the government.

highlights: Ports and offshore resources drive regional rivalry

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Control of Offshore Assets
frictionVectors.details: Federal, regional, and security authorities do not exercise uniform control across Somalia's maritime space, complicating fisheries protection, offshore licensing, and revenue allocation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, neighboring countries, and other partners compete for influence over ports, military access, and logistics, often intersecting with disputes over territorial sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and battery minerals. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation, but capital, electricity, and regulatory constraints limit bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Power and freight infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port dysfunction continue to weaken sovereign control over mining and export chains. Private investment and foreign-linked logistics partnerships are increasingly necessary to maintain throughput.

highlights: Oil revenues remain hostage to transit risk

frictionVectors.title: Sudan pipeline dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan to export most of its crude. Disruptions, transit negotiations, and competing external patrons leave Juba with little control over its primary revenue stream.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and security-linked intermediaries retain substantial influence over production, payments, and infrastructure. Weak institutions and elite competition limit the conversion of resource income into broad national sovereignty.

highlights: War fragments control of extractive assets

frictionVectors.title: Gold smuggling and external patrons
frictionVectors.details: Gold flows through informal and cross-border networks that benefit armed factions and foreign intermediaries. Gulf, regional, and Russian-linked commercial interests compete for access while state oversight remains severely degraded.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea corridor, oil-export infrastructure, and Port Sudan have become strategic leverage points in the conflict. Damage, blockade risks, and rival claims over customs and transit revenues further erode sovereign control.

highlights: Ports and railways become strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for greater state participation, local processing, and revenue capture in gold and critical-mineral projects. Foreign investors remain important, creating tension between sovereignty goals and the need for capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Indian, and Western actors are competing for influence over Dar es Salaam port, rail, and energy corridors. These projects can strengthen Tanzania's leverage but may also embed long-term dependence on external finance and operators.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's port and neighboring trade corridors are valuable infrastructure assets, but their expansion depends heavily on foreign finance, shipping networks, and regional demand. External commercial influence therefore remains substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate and security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate revenues and mining infrastructure remain central to resource sovereignty, while insecurity spreading south from the Sahel raises protection costs. International security and commercial partners have growing leverage over key logistics and extractive operations.

frictionVectors.title: Migration-for-finance bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European funding and political engagement remain closely tied to Tunisia's role in containing irregular migration. This gives external partners leverage over domestic policy while economic distress limits Tunisian negotiating power.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported hydrocarbons and constrained state finances weaken sovereignty over energy planning. Declining phosphate performance further reduces export earnings and fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP sovereignty conflict
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline promises revenue and export capacity but leaves the country exposed to foreign operators, financing conditions, sanctions risk, and environmental opposition. Project delays could increase Uganda's dependence on external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-influence exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, power, and industrial projects support connectivity but increase repayment and strategic-dependence concerns. Kampala is balancing Chinese capital against Western pressure over governance and human-rights issues.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors to seek better terms in copper and battery-mineral projects. Limited domestic refining capacity still leaves value capture and technology control largely external.

frictionVectors.title: Power-sector bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages and climate-linked droughts constrain mining output and industrial sovereignty. Emergency imports and new generation projects risk creating fresh dependence on neighboring grids and foreign developers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral value chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium and other mining operations, while Harare seeks domestic processing and tighter export controls. Weak capital access and limited refining capacity reduce Zimbabwe's leverage over pricing and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and currency instability restrict access to affordable external finance and complicate infrastructure investment. The resulting dependence on politically aligned investors can trade short-term liquidity for long-term resource concessions.
